text: What happens, step by step, when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?
answer: First the browser parses the URL and checks its own cache, because if it has a fresh copy of the page it may not need the network at all. Otherwise it needs an IP address, so DNS resolution kicks in, checking the browser cache, the operating system cache, then a recursive resolver that walks from the root servers down to the authoritative name server. With the IP in hand, it opens a TCP connection using the three-way handshake, and for HTTPS it does a TLS handshake to verify the certificate and agree on encryption keys. Then it sends the HTTP request, which may be answered by a CDN or proxy cache before it ever reaches the origin server, and it gets back a status, headers and a body. Finally the browser renders: it parses HTML into the DOM, parses CSS into style rules, runs JavaScript, which can change both, then does layout and paint. Caching headers decide what gets reused next time.

text: Explain the difference between a process and a thread.
answer: A process is a running program with its own isolated address space, file handles and other resources, while a thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and all threads in a process share the same memory. That difference drives everything else. Creating a process and switching between processes costs more, because the operating system has to set up and change the address space, whereas threads are lighter to create and cheaper to switch. Communication differs too: processes need inter-process mechanisms like pipes, sockets or shared memory segments, while threads can simply read and write the same variables, which is fast but means you need locks or other synchronization to avoid race conditions. I would use processes when I want isolation, so one crash does not take down the others, or to run separate programs. I would use threads when tasks need to share a lot of data or run concurrently with low overhead inside one application.

text: How does an index speed up a database query, and what does it cost?
answer: An index is a separate sorted data structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to the location of the matching rows. Without one, the database has to do a full table scan, checking every row, which is linear in the table size. With a B-tree, it walks down a shallow tree in logarithmic time and then reads only the rows it needs, and because the keys are sorted it also helps with range queries and ordering. The cost is that every insert, update or delete touching indexed columns must also maintain the index, so writes get slower, and the index takes up disk space and memory. So I index columns that appear often in where clauses, joins and sorts, and that are selective enough to be worth it. For composite indexes, order matters: an index on customer and then date helps queries filtering by customer, or customer and date, but generally not date alone. I put equality columns first, then range columns.

text: Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases, and how you would choose between them.
answer: SQL databases store data in tables with a fixed schema, and relationships are expressed through foreign keys and joins, while NoSQL is a broad family covering document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores, usually with more flexible schemas. On consistency, relational databases give you strong ACID transactions across multiple rows and tables. Many NoSQL systems historically focused on single-record atomicity and offer eventual or tunable consistency, although several now support multi-document transactions. On scaling, SQL databases traditionally scale vertically and with read replicas, while many NoSQL stores are built to scale horizontally by partitioning data across nodes, though that is not an absolute rule. I choose based on access patterns. If I have related data, need ad hoc queries and care about correctness, like orders and payments, I default to something like Postgres. If I have huge volumes with simple, predictable lookups by key, like session data or event feeds, a NoSQL store can fit better.

text: What are REST principles, and when might you choose something else, like GraphQL or gRPC?
answer: REST is an architectural style where you model your system as resources identified by URLs and act on them with standard HTTP verbs, like GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update and DELETE to remove. It is stateless, so each request carries everything the server needs, which makes horizontal scaling easier. Status codes communicate outcomes in a standard way: two hundreds for success, four hundreds for client errors, five hundreds for server errors. I would reach for GraphQL when clients have varied data needs, such as a mobile app and a web app, because they can request exactly the fields they want in one round trip. The trade-off is that HTTP caching gets harder, since most queries go through a single POST endpoint, and you have to guard against expensive queries. gRPC suits internal service-to-service calls: it uses HTTP two and Protocol Buffers for compact, fast messages and strongly typed contracts, but browsers cannot call it directly without a proxy.

text: Explain how the JavaScript event loop works.
expected: why blocking code is a problem
answer: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, with a call stack that holds the functions currently executing. Asynchronous work, like timers or network calls, is handled by the browser or by Node, and when it finishes, its callback is placed in a queue. The event loop's job is to wait until the call stack is empty, then take the next task. There are two kinds of queue. Tasks, sometimes called macrotasks, include setTimeout callbacks and input events. Microtasks include promise callbacks and queueMicrotask. After each task finishes, the whole microtask queue is drained before the next task runs. So if I schedule a setTimeout with zero delay and then a resolved promise's callback, the promise callback runs first, even though the timer was scheduled earlier. Blocking code is a problem because while a long synchronous loop runs, nothing else can: the page stops rendering and responding, and a Node server stalls every request. So I would move heavy work to a worker thread or break it into chunks.

text: What is a race condition? Give an example and explain how to prevent it.
answer: A race condition is when the outcome of a program depends on the timing of concurrent operations that touch shared state. A classic example is two requests withdrawing from an account holding one hundred dollars. Both read the balance, both see one hundred, both subtract, and each writes its own result, so one update is lost. There are a few ways to prevent it. A lock or mutex makes the read and write happen one at a time; it is simple to reason about, but it reduces concurrency and can cause deadlocks. Atomic operations, like compare-and-swap or an increment done in a single SQL update statement, are fast and need no lock, but they only cover small, single-value changes. Database transactions, with the right isolation level or row locks, protect multi-step changes, at the cost of contention and possibly retries when conflicts occur. I would pick the narrowest tool that works, and use a transaction when the state lives in the database.

text: How would you approach debugging a web service that has become slow in production?
expected: narrowing down: database, network, CPU, memory
answer: First I confirm the problem and measure it: which endpoints are slow, since when, how many users are affected, and whether it is the average or the tail, like the ninety-ninth percentile. I also check what changed, such as a deploy, a config change or a traffic spike. Then I go to the metrics, logs and distributed traces to see where the time goes in a slow request, and I narrow it down layer by layer: the database, with slow queries or lock contention; the network and downstream dependencies; CPU saturation; and memory pressure, like garbage collection pauses or swapping. If users are hurting, I mitigate before I fully understand it, choosing something safe and reversible, like rolling back, scaling out, or turning off a feature flag. Once things are stable, I find the actual root cause, fix it, and prevent a repeat with a blameless review, a better alert or dashboard, and load tests that would have caught it.

text: Explain what happens during a database transaction and what ACID means.
answer: A transaction groups several operations into one logical unit, so you begin it, do your reads and writes, and then either commit or roll back. Take a bank transfer that debits one account and credits another. Atomicity means both happen or neither does, so a crash halfway leaves no money missing. Consistency means the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints, such as a balance that must not go negative. Isolation means concurrent transactions behave as if they ran alone, without seeing each other's partial work, and the degree is configurable through isolation levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable, where stricter levels prevent more anomalies but reduce concurrency. Durability means once a commit is acknowledged, the change survives a crash, usually because it was first written to a write-ahead log on disk. While the transaction runs, the database typically uses locks or multi-version concurrency control to keep transactions apart.

text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization? How would you implement them in a web app?
expected: role or permission checks on the server
answer: Authentication answers who you are, and authorization answers what you are allowed to do. Authentication happens first, and authorization is checked on each action afterwards. For login, I never store passwords directly. I store a salted hash from a deliberately slow algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt, so a leaked database is hard to crack. After login there are two common options. With sessions, the server stores state and the browser holds a random session ID in a secure, HttpOnly cookie, which makes revocation easy. With tokens, such as signed JWTs, the server can verify them without a lookup, which suits APIs and multiple services, but revoking them is harder, so I would keep them short-lived and add refresh tokens. For authorization, I would use roles or finer-grained permissions and enforce them on the server, in middleware or a policy layer, on every request, and also check ownership of the specific resource. Hiding a button in the UI is only cosmetic, not security.

text: What are common web security vulnerabilities and how do you defend against them?
answer: The ones I think about first are injection, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery and broken access control. Injection, like SQL injection, is when user input gets interpreted as code, so I use parameterized queries and validate input. Cross-site scripting is when an attacker gets their script running in another user's browser. The defense is context-aware output encoding, which modern frameworks do by default, sanitizing any HTML I accept, and adding a Content Security Policy. CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request with their cookies, so I use anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies. Broken access control is when a user can reach data that is not theirs, for example by changing an ID in the URL. I defend with server-side authorization checks on every request, denying by default, and tests for those rules. At a team level, I would add secure defaults, dependency scanning and security reviews, since this is a process problem as much as a coding one.

text: How do you decide what to test, and at which level: unit, integration or end-to-end?
expected: cost and speed of each level
answer: I think of it as a pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of end-to-end tests, though the exact shape depends on the system. The reasoning is cost and speed. Unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint failures, but they do not prove that parts work together. Integration tests, which use a real database or service boundary, are slower but catch wiring and query problems. End-to-end tests are the most realistic, but they are slow, expensive to maintain and prone to flakiness. Within that, I focus on risk: how bad would a failure be, how likely is it, and how complex is the code? So a pricing calculation with many edge cases gets thorough unit tests, a repository that saves orders gets integration tests against a real database, and the checkout flow gets one or two end-to-end tests covering the critical path. I skip trivial getters, and I always add a regression test when fixing a bug.

text: Explain how caching works in a web application and what can go wrong with it.
expected: cache layers: browser, CDN, application, database
answer: Caching stores a copy of data closer to where it is needed, and it happens in layers. The browser caches based on HTTP headers like Cache-Control and ETag, a CDN caches static assets and sometimes responses near users, the application caches computed results in memory or in something like Redis, and the database has its own buffer pool in memory. The hard part is invalidation. Options include a time to live, deleting the key whenever the data changes, write-through where writes update the cache and the store together, and versioned keys, which work well for static assets. Stale data means users see old values, so I decide up front how much staleness each piece of data can tolerate. A stampede happens when a popular key expires and many requests hit the database at once; I handle that with request coalescing or a lock, plus jittered expiry. And memory is finite, so I need an eviction policy like least recently used, plus hit rate monitoring.

text: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when would you use each?
answer: Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they treat history differently. Merge keeps both histories as they happened and adds a merge commit with two parents, so the history is accurate but can look busier. Rebase takes my commits and replays them on top of the target branch, creating new commits with new hashes, which gives a clean, linear history. Conflicts differ as well. With a merge, I resolve all conflicts once, in the merge commit. With a rebase, commits are applied one at a time, so I may have to resolve conflicts at each step, sometimes the same one repeatedly. I usually rebase my own local feature branch onto main to keep it up to date, then merge it through a pull request, but I follow whatever convention the team has agreed on, such as squash merging. The key rule is never to rebase shared history, because rewriting commits others have based work on forces them to reconcile diverged branches.

text: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
answer: The core difference is what gets virtualized. A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system with its own kernel on top of a hypervisor, which virtualizes the hardware. A container is just an isolated group of processes that shares the host's kernel, using Linux namespaces for isolation and control groups for resource limits. Because of that, containers are smaller, often megabytes rather than gigabytes, and start in seconds or less, whereas a VM typically has to boot a whole operating system. The trade-off is isolation. VMs have a stronger security boundary, because a kernel vulnerability on a shared host can affect all its containers, and they can run a different operating system from the host. So I would use containers for packaging microservices, keeping environments consistent across development and CI, and running many services densely with an orchestrator like Kubernetes. I would use VMs for strong isolation between tenants, for legacy applications, or when I need a different kernel.

text: Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning, with examples.
answer: The key difference is labels. In supervised learning, each training example comes with the correct answer, and the model learns to map inputs to that output. That splits into classification, where you predict a category, like spam or not spam, and regression, where you predict a number, like a house price. In unsupervised learning there are no labels, so the algorithm looks for structure in the data itself. The standard example is clustering, like using k-means to group customers by purchasing behavior, where nobody has told it what the groups are. Evaluation differs a lot too. With supervised learning, I can compare predictions against known answers on held-out data, using accuracy, precision and recall for classification, or mean squared error for regression. With unsupervised learning, there is no ground truth, so I rely on internal measures like the silhouette score, which shows how well separated the clusters are, plus whether the results make sense and are useful to the business.

text: How would you handle missing values in a dataset?
answer: Before changing anything, I want to understand why the values are missing. Did a sensor fail at random, or did a certain group of people skip a question? Values missing at random and values missing for a reason tied to the outcome need different treatment. I also look at how much is missing and in which columns. Then I decide between dropping and imputing. Dropping rows is reasonable when very few are affected and they look random, and I might drop a column that is mostly empty. Otherwise I impute, with the median or mode for simple cases, or a model-based method like k-nearest neighbors, sometimes with a flag column marking that the value was missing. Either choice can add bias. If, say, high earners skip the income question, dropping them or filling in the mean skews the results. Finally, I check the effect by comparing distributions and model performance across approaches, and I fit imputation on training data only to avoid leakage.

text: What is overfitting, and how do you detect and prevent it?
answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the noise and quirks of its training data rather than the underlying pattern, so it does well on data it has seen and poorly on new data. The main signal is a gap between training and validation performance: training error keeps falling while validation error stalls or starts rising. To get a reliable estimate, I use cross-validation, like k-fold, where the data is split into k parts and each takes a turn as the validation set, which also tells me whether performance is stable. For prevention, I have a few tools. Regularization, such as L1 or L2 penalties, dropout in neural networks, or early stopping, limits how much the model can fit noise. More data helps, including augmentation where that is valid. Simpler models, with fewer features or shallower trees, reduce capacity. I also keep a final test set untouched, because repeated tuning against validation data can quietly overfit to it as well.

text: Explain the main types of SQL joins and when you would use each.
expected: left and right joins keep unmatched rows
choosing based on which rows must be kept
answer: A join combines rows from two tables based on a related column, and the main types differ in which rows they keep. Say we have customers and orders. An inner join returns only rows that match on both sides, so just customers who have orders. A left join keeps every row from the left table, filling in nulls where there is no match, so I get all customers, including those with no orders. A right join is the mirror image, keeping every row from the right table, and in practice most people just swap the tables and write a left join. A full outer join keeps everything from both sides, matched where possible, with nulls on either side, which is useful for comparing two datasets to find what is missing from each. So my choice comes down to which rows must be kept. If I only want matches, I use inner. If one table must be complete, I use left.

text: What is database normalization, and when would you denormalize?
expected: cost of keeping copies in sync
answer: Normalization is organizing a relational schema so each fact is stored in one place. The aim is to reduce duplication and avoid update anomalies, where for example a customer's address appears on every order, so changing it means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the data inconsistent. To fix that, you split data into related tables: customers in one, orders in another, linked by a foreign key. Normal forms like first, second and third describe this progressively, and third normal form is a typical target for transactional systems. I would denormalize when reads are very frequent and joins have become the bottleneck, like storing a comment count on a post, or building a reporting table. I would do it only after measuring, and after trying indexes. The cost is keeping copies in sync, through application code, triggers or background jobs, which adds write overhead and the risk of drift. So I start normalized and denormalize deliberately.

text: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you detect and fix it?
expected: one query per row of a previous result
detecting it through query logs or tracing
fixing it with joins, eager loading or batching
answer: The N plus one problem is when code runs one query to fetch a list and then one extra query for each row in that result. Say I load one hundred orders and then, in a loop, fetch each order's customer: that is one hundred and one queries instead of one or two. It is especially common with ORMs, because lazy loading hides the queries behind what looks like a simple property access, so it works fine in development with small data and then gets slow in production. To detect it, I look at query logs for many near-identical queries in one request, use application tracing to spot a long run of similar database spans, or use tools that flag it automatically. Tests can also assert a query count. To fix it, I fetch the related data up front with a join or the ORM's eager loading, or batch it into a single query using an in clause, which is what the DataLoader pattern does in GraphQL.

text: How would you investigate and speed up a slow SQL query?
expected: spotting full scans and bad join order
rewriting the query or reducing the data returned
answer: I would start by measuring, capturing the current run time and how often the query runs, ideally with realistic data volumes. Then I read the execution plan, using EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres, which actually runs the query and shows real timings and row counts. I look for full table scans on large tables, a bad join order, expensive sorts, and big gaps between estimated and actual rows, which suggest stale statistics. If a filter or join column has no usable index, I add one, or fix an existing one, for example a composite index in the wrong order, or a function wrapped around a column that stops the index being used. If indexing is not enough, I rewrite the query: selecting only needed columns instead of select star, filtering earlier, paginating, or replacing a correlated subquery. Then I measure again on the same data, and I check that any new index does not hurt write performance too much.

text: What are transaction isolation levels, and what problems does each one prevent?
expected: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads
choosing a level for the workload
answer: Isolation levels define how much concurrent transactions can see of each other, and they are framed around three anomalies. A dirty read is seeing another transaction's uncommitted data. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice and getting different values, because someone committed in between. A phantom read is running the same range query twice and getting different rows. In the SQL standard, read committed prevents dirty reads; repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads; and serializable prevents all three, making the outcome equivalent to some serial order. Real databases vary: repeatable read in Postgres is snapshot isolation, which also stops phantoms but can allow write skew. Stronger isolation costs more, through lock contention or aborted transactions that must be retried, so throughput drops. For most web workloads I default to read committed and add explicit row locks where needed. For invariants across rows, like financial rules, I use serializable with retry logic. For reports, a consistent snapshot works well.

text: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?
expected: pessimistic locks data before changing it
optimistic checks a version when writing
choice depends on how often conflicts happen
answer: Pessimistic locking assumes a conflict is likely, so it locks the data before changing it. In SQL that is typically select for update: other writers wait until the transaction commits or rolls back. That guarantees no conflicting change, but it reduces concurrency, holds connections open, and can lead to deadlocks. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare, so no lock is held while working. Each row has a version number or timestamp. I read the row, remember the version, and when writing I update only where the version still matches, incrementing it. If zero rows were updated, someone else got there first, so I retry by re-reading and reapplying the change, or I report the conflict to the user. The choice depends on how often conflicts happen. With low contention, like users editing their own profiles, optimistic gives better throughput, and it suits long user interactions where holding a lock would be impractical. With high contention, like many buyers of the last tickets, retries waste work, so pessimistic is often better.

text: What are replication and sharding, and what problem does each one solve?
expected: replication copies data for reads and availability
sharding splits data to scale writes and storage
answer: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple nodes. That gives you availability, because a replica can take over if the primary fails, and read scaling, because reads can go to replicas. Its main catch is replication lag: with asynchronous replication, a replica can fall behind, so a user might not see their own write unless I route that read to the primary. Sharding solves a different problem. It splits the data so each node holds a subset, which scales writes and storage beyond what one machine can handle. The critical decision is the shard key: it should distribute load evenly and match the main query pattern, like a tenant ID, because a poor key creates hot shards. Sharding brings real complexity. Cross-shard queries and transactions are slow or hard, and rebalancing when adding nodes means moving data, which consistent hashing can reduce. I would exhaust indexing, caching and read replicas first, and in practice the two are combined, with each shard replicated.

text: What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST?
expected: POST creates or triggers an action
answer: All three send data to the server, but they mean different things. POST is the general one: it creates a new resource, usually at a collection URL where the server picks the ID, or it triggers an action, like sending an email. PUT replaces a resource entirely at a specific URL, so I send the full representation, and any field I leave out is effectively removed or reset. PATCH applies a partial change, so I send only the fields that should change, like updating just a user's email. The important difference is idempotency. PUT is idempotent, because sending the same full replacement twice leaves the same state as sending it once. POST is not idempotent, so sending it twice might create two orders. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent: setting a field to a value is safe to repeat, but an operation like incrementing a counter by one is not. That affects whether clients can safely retry.

text: What does it mean for an API operation to be idempotent, and why does it matter?
expected: repeating it has the same effect as doing it once
answer: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect on the server as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are defined that way in HTTP, whereas POST is not. It matters because networks are unreliable. If a client sends a request and times out, it cannot tell whether the server processed it, so the natural response is to retry, and automatic retries also happen in client libraries, gateways and queues. Payments are the classic example. If a charge succeeds but the response is lost, a naive retry bills the customer twice. The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique ID for the logical operation and sends it with each attempt. The server stores the key with the result, ideally in the same transaction as the work, and a repeat returns the saved result instead of charging again. A unique constraint on the key handles concurrent duplicates, and keys can expire after a retention window.

text: What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination, and which would you choose?
expected: offset slows down on deep pages
cursor cannot jump to an arbitrary page
answer: Offset pagination tells the database to skip a number of rows and return the next batch, like limit twenty, offset one thousand. Cursor pagination, also called keyset pagination, has the client send a marker for the last row it saw, such as its created time and ID, and the query asks for rows after that value using an index. Offset is simple and lets users jump to page fifty, but it has two problems. Deep pages get slower, because the database still has to walk through all the skipped rows. And if rows are inserted or deleted between requests, they shift, so users see duplicates or miss items. Cursor stays fast at any depth with a suitable index, and it stays stable under changes. Its limitation is that it cannot jump to an arbitrary page, only move next or previous. So I would choose cursor for feeds, infinite scroll and large or fast-changing data, and offset for small admin tables where page numbers matter.

text: How would you version an API without breaking existing clients?
expected: versioning in the URL or a header
monitoring who still uses the old version
answer: My first goal is to avoid needing a new version at all. Backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields or new endpoints, do not break clients, provided clients ignore fields they do not recognize. So I never remove or rename a field, or change its type or meaning, in place. When a breaking change is truly needed, I introduce a new version, either in the URL, like slash v2, or in a header, such as a custom header or the Accept header. URL versioning is explicit and easy to route and debug, while header versioning keeps URLs stable but is less visible. I prefer the URL for public APIs. Then I need a clear deprecation policy: announce it, publish a migration guide, give a timeline such as six or twelve months, and signal it with deprecation headers. Before retiring anything, I monitor traffic per version and per client, so I know who still uses the old version and can contact them directly.

text: What is the difference between TCP and UDP, and when would you use each?
expected: reliable ordered delivery vs best effort
examples such as web traffic and live video
answer: TCP is connection-oriented: the two sides set up a connection with a handshake before sending any data. UDP is connectionless, so you just send datagrams without any setup. The bigger difference is delivery. TCP gives you reliable, ordered delivery: it numbers bytes, acknowledges them, retransmits anything lost, and does flow and congestion control. UDP is best effort, so packets can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order, and the application has to deal with that if it cares. All of that makes TCP heavier, with more overhead and more latency, especially when one lost packet holds up everything behind it. UDP has a small header and no waiting, so it is faster and lighter. I would use TCP when every byte must arrive correctly, like web traffic, APIs, file transfers and email. I would use UDP when timeliness matters more than perfection, like live video, voice calls and online games, where a late packet is useless anyway.

text: How does HTTPS keep traffic between a browser and a server secure?
answer: HTTPS is HTTP running over TLS, and the security comes from the TLS handshake before any application data is sent. First, the server presents a certificate containing its public key and domain name, signed by a certificate authority. The browser checks that signature against its built-in list of trusted authorities, along with the domain and expiry date, so it knows it is talking to the real server. Then the two sides do an asymmetric key exchange, typically ephemeral Diffie-Hellman in modern TLS, to agree on a shared secret without ever sending it over the wire. Asymmetric cryptography is slow, so that secret is only used to derive symmetric session keys, and all the actual data is encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher like AES. This protects against eavesdropping, since observers only see ciphertext, and against tampering, because each record carries an authentication tag, so any modification is detected. An observer can still see the destination IP address, though.

text: What is CORS, and why does the browser enforce it?
expected: server allows origins through response headers
it is enforced by the browser, not the server
answer: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy, which says a script from one origin, meaning the scheme, host and port, generally cannot read responses from another origin. That exists so a malicious site cannot use your logged-in browser session to read data from your bank. CORS is the controlled way to relax that. The server lists what it allows through response headers, mainly Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and the browser checks that header and decides whether to give the response to the script. For requests that are not simple, such as those with custom headers, a JSON content type, or methods like PUT or DELETE, the browser first sends a preflight, an OPTIONS request asking what is permitted, and only proceeds if the server agrees. The important thing is that the browser enforces this, not the server. A curl command or another backend ignores it completely, so CORS is no substitute for authentication, and it protects users rather than protecting your API.

text: How do WebSockets differ from polling and server-sent events?
expected: server-sent events stream one way from the server
WebSockets are a two-way persistent connection
answer: The main difference is who can talk and how the connection is used. With polling, the client simply repeats HTTP requests on an interval asking whether anything changed, which is easy to build but wasteful and adds latency. Long polling improves that a little by holding each request open until there is data. Server-sent events keep one HTTP response open so the server can stream events one way to the browser, with reconnection built in. WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel, so either side can send a message at any time with very little overhead per message. The cost of those last two is that every open connection uses memory and a file descriptor on the server, and load balancers and deployments have to cope with long-lived connections. So I choose by use case: polling for infrequent updates, server-sent events for feeds and notifications, and WebSockets for chat, multiplayer games or collaborative editing.

text: What does a load balancer do, and how does it decide where to send a request?
answer: A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and distributes incoming traffic across them, so no single machine is overloaded and one failure does not take the service down. It runs health checks against each server and stops sending requests to any that fail. To pick a target, it uses an algorithm. Round robin just cycles through the servers, least connections picks the one with the fewest active requests, which suits uneven workloads, and hashing maps something like the client address or a key to a server, so the same client tends to land in the same place. There is also a distinction between layers. A layer four balancer routes on IP addresses and ports and is very fast, while a layer seven balancer understands HTTP, so it can route by path, host or headers. Sticky sessions pin a user to one server, which helps with in-memory session state, but they weaken even distribution, so I would rather move sessions to a shared store.

text: Compare session-based authentication with JSON Web Tokens.
expected: where the credential is stored in the browser
answer: The core difference is where the state lives. With sessions, the server stores the session data and the browser only holds a random identifier, usually in a cookie, so each request needs a lookup in something like Redis. With a JSON Web Token, the server issues a signed token containing the claims, and it verifies the signature without any lookup, which is convenient across many services. The trade-off is revocation. Deleting a session logs someone out instantly, but a token stays valid until it expires unless you add a deny list, which brings server-side state back. That is why tokens are kept short-lived, often minutes, and paired with a longer-lived refresh token that can be rotated and revoked. Storage in the browser matters too. I prefer an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie because script cannot read it, whereas local storage is exposed to cross-site scripting. Cookies do need CSRF protection, though. For a typical web app, I usually default to sessions.

text: What is SQL injection, and how do you prevent it?
expected: user input treated as part of the query
input validation as an extra layer
answer: SQL injection happens when user input gets treated as part of the query rather than as data, usually because a string was concatenated into the SQL. Say a login form builds a query from the username field. An attacker can type a quote followed by their own SQL and change what the statement does, bypassing the login, reading other tables or even deleting data. The main defense is parameterized queries, also called prepared statements. The query structure is sent separately and the values are bound to placeholders, so the database never interprets them as SQL. Most ORMs do this for you, as long as you avoid raw string building. On top of that, I would validate input as an extra layer, for example checking types, lengths and allowed values, but that does not replace parameters. Finally, I would give the application a least-privilege database account, with only the permissions it needs, so that if something does slip through, the damage is limited.

text: How should an application store user passwords?
expected: never plain text or reversible encryption
slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2
why fast hashes are not enough
answer: Passwords should never be stored in plain text, and they should not use reversible encryption either, because if the database and key leak, every password is exposed. Instead, I store a one-way hash and, at login, hash the submitted password and compare the results. The hash has to be a deliberately slow one designed for passwords, such as bcrypt or Argon2, with Argon2id being a good modern default. Fast hashes like SHA-256 or MD5 are not enough, because they were built for speed, so an attacker with GPUs can try billions of guesses per second against a stolen database. A slow, tunable work factor makes each guess expensive, and Argon2 also costs memory, which makes GPU attacks harder. Each password also gets its own unique random salt, stored alongside the hash. That means two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables stop working. I would use a well-tested library for this, and never write my own.

text: What is the difference between cross-site scripting and cross-site request forgery, and how do you defend against each?
expected: XSS runs attacker script in the page
CSRF abuses the victim's logged-in session
output escaping and content security policy
answer: These two attacks exploit trust in opposite directions. Cross-site scripting means an attacker gets their script to run inside your page, usually because user content was rendered unsafely, so the script can read page data, act as the user or steal any token that script can reach. Cross-site request forgery does not run code in your page at all. It abuses the victim's logged-in session: a malicious site makes the browser send a request to your app, and the browser attaches the cookies automatically, so the action looks legitimate. To defend against cross-site scripting, I escape output according to its context, avoid injecting raw HTML, and add a content security policy that restricts which scripts can run. HttpOnly cookies also limit the damage. To defend against request forgery, I use CSRF tokens that a foreign site cannot read, and SameSite cookies so the browser does not send them on cross-site requests. One thing worth noting is that cross-site scripting can defeat CSRF tokens, so fixing it comes first.

text: What is a deadlock, and how do you prevent one?
expected: tasks waiting on each other's locks
answer: A deadlock is when two or more tasks are stuck forever because each one holds a lock the other is waiting for. For example, one thread holds lock A and wants lock B, while another holds B and wants A. Four conditions all have to be true for this to happen: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait. Prevention means breaking at least one of them. The most practical approach is consistent lock ordering, so every thread acquires locks in the same global order and a cycle can never form. I also try to hold locks for as short a time as possible and avoid calling external code while holding one. Timeouts help too: using a try-lock with a timeout, a task can release what it has, back off and retry. Databases take the detection route, finding cycles in the wait-for graph and aborting one transaction as the victim, so application code should be ready to retry.

text: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
expected: stack holds function calls and local values
lifetime and who frees the memory
answer: Stack memory holds function calls and their local values. Each time a function is called, a frame is pushed containing its parameters, local variables and return address, and when the function returns, that frame is popped. The heap is a larger area used for dynamically allocated objects, meaning things whose size or lifetime is not tied to a single function call. Lifetime is the key difference. Stack memory is freed automatically when the function returns, whereas heap memory lives until it is released, either by the programmer, as in C with malloc and free, or by a garbage collector, as in Java or JavaScript. The stack is faster because allocating is just moving a pointer, and it has good cache locality. The heap is slower because the allocator has to find space, and it can become fragmented. The stack is also much smaller, often only a few megabytes per thread, which is why very deep recursion causes a stack overflow.

text: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
expected: concurrency is managing several tasks at once
parallelism is running them at the same moment
answer: Concurrency is about managing several tasks at once, so they make progress during overlapping periods of time, even if only one is actually running at any given instant. A single-core machine can do this by switching between tasks. Parallelism means tasks are literally running at the same moment, which needs multiple cores or processors. I like the kitchen analogy: one cook juggling three dishes is concurrent, while three cooks each making a dish is parallel. Concurrency is about structuring the work, and parallelism is about executing it simultaneously. The distinction matters when you pick a tool. For input and output bound work, like waiting on network calls or a database, concurrency is usually enough, because tasks spend most of their time waiting, and that is why Node handles many connections on one event loop. For CPU-bound work, like image processing or heavy calculations, concurrency alone will not speed things up, so you need real parallelism through multiple threads or processes running across several cores.

text: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking I/O, and how does it affect a server?
expected: blocking holds a thread while waiting
CPU-heavy work is still a problem
answer: With blocking input and output, a call does not return until the operation finishes, so the thread sits idle while waiting on the disk or network. With non-blocking input and output, the call returns right away, the program carries on with other work, and it gets notified when the result is ready, typically through the operating system's mechanisms such as epoll on Linux. This shapes server design. The classic thread-per-request model is simple to reason about, but each waiting request holds a thread, and threads cost memory and context switches, so thread pools limit concurrency under slow dependencies. An event loop, as in Node or nginx, can serve thousands of idle or waiting connections with very few threads, since none of them sit blocked. The catch is CPU-heavy work, which is still a problem: non-blocking only helps with waiting, so a long computation on the event loop stalls every other request. I would move that work to worker threads or a separate service.

text: What causes a memory leak in a long-running service, and how would you find one?
answer: Even with a garbage collector, leaks happen, because the collector only frees what is unreachable. So a leak in a managed language usually means objects are kept reachable by mistake. The common causes are caches with no size limit or expiry, event listeners or subscriptions that are never removed, global variables or module-level maps that keep growing, timers that are never cleared, and closures holding on to large objects. To find one, I start by watching memory grow over time on a dashboard. A healthy service shows a sawtooth that returns to a stable baseline after collection, while a leak shows that baseline steadily climbing, often until an out-of-memory restart. Then I take heap snapshots a while apart, ideally under realistic load, and compare them to see which object types keep increasing. In Node, I would use Chrome DevTools for this. The retainer path shows what is holding those objects, which usually points to the exact code. Once it is fixed, I confirm the baseline has flattened.

text: What are the core ideas of object-oriented programming?
answer: Object-oriented programming organizes code around objects that combine data and behavior, and it rests on four ideas. Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and exposing controlled methods. For example, a bank account keeps its balance hidden, and you can only change it through deposit and withdraw, which enforce the rules. Abstraction means exposing what something does while hiding how it does it. When I call a send method on an email client, I do not need to know about the protocol underneath. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another one, so a savings account can extend a general account and add interest. Polymorphism means different types can respond to the same call in their own way. Say a payment processor calls a charge method on any payment type, and a card and a digital wallet each do something different, while the calling code stays the same. Together, these make code easier to maintain and extend.

text: Explain the SOLID principles and how they affect real code.
expected: knows when applying them is overkill
answer: SOLID is five design principles. Single responsibility means a class should have one reason to change. Open-closed means you can add behavior through extension rather than by editing tested code. Liskov substitution means a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected. Interface segregation means small, focused interfaces rather than one large one that forces clients to depend on methods they do not use. Dependency inversion means high-level code depends on abstractions rather than concrete details. As a concrete example, say an order service sends receipts. If it builds the email itself, it has two responsibilities and is tied to one provider. If it instead depends on a notifier interface that is passed in, I can add text messages without changing it and use a fake in tests. That said, these are guidelines rather than laws. Applying them is overkill for a small script or code with only one implementation, where extra layers just add indirection, so I wait until real change justifies them.

text: When would you prefer composition over inheritance?
answer: I would prefer composition in most cases, and I reach for inheritance only when there is a genuine is-a relationship. A useful test is is-a versus has-a: a car has an engine, so composition fits, while a savings account really is an account. The problem with inheritance is tight coupling. A subclass depends on its parent's internals, so in a deep hierarchy a small change at the top can break classes far below it, and behaviors that cut across branches get awkward to share. With composition, an object holds small collaborators behind interfaces, which also lets you swap behavior at runtime. For example, a notifier can be given a different delivery strategy or retry policy without creating a new subclass for every combination. Inheritance still fits when subclasses truly honor the parent's contract, when the hierarchy is shallow and stable, or when a framework expects it, like extending a base exception class. Then the code reuse is natural and the coupling is acceptable.

text: How do you decide between a monolith and microservices?
expected: modular monolith as a middle path
answer: I usually start with a monolith unless there is a clear reason not to. Its simplicity is a big advantage: one codebase, one deployment, in-process calls, easy local transactions and straightforward debugging. Microservices earn their place when you need independent deployment and scaling, so a team can release without coordinating with everyone, and a heavy component can scale alone. But they carry real operational and network cost: service discovery, observability, partial failures, latency, versioned contracts and data consistency across services. So the deciding factors are team size and domain boundaries. If several teams keep getting in each other's way and the domains are well understood, splitting makes sense. With a small team or a domain that is still shifting, you risk drawing the wrong boundaries and getting a distributed monolith. A good middle path is a modular monolith, with strict internal module boundaries and separate data ownership, deployed as one unit. Later, a module with real need can be extracted into a service.

text: Explain the CAP theorem and what it means for a real system.
expected: the real choice happens during a partition
answer: The CAP theorem says that a distributed data store cannot guarantee all three of consistency, availability and partition tolerance at once. Consistency here means every read sees the latest write, availability means every request to a working node gets a response, and partition tolerance means the system keeps operating when the network splits. Since partitions are unavoidable in real systems, the real choice only happens during a partition: either refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer them and risk stale data. Systems like etcd and ZooKeeper choose consistency, which suits coordination, leader election and things like payments or inventory, where wrong data is worse than an error. Systems like Cassandra, in their typical configurations, choose availability, which suits carts, feeds or activity data. Those rely on eventual consistency, meaning replicas converge over time as updates spread and conflicts are resolved, for example by last write wins. In practice, I make this decision per feature, and also weigh the latency trade-off that exists even when there is no partition.

text: Why would you put a message queue between two services, and what delivery guarantees should you expect?
answer: The main reasons to add a queue are decoupling and absorbing load. The producer can hand off work and move on without waiting for the consumer or even needing it to be up, and traffic spikes build up in the queue rather than overwhelming the downstream service, which also lets consumers scale independently. On delivery guarantees, at-most-once means a message may be lost but is never redelivered. At-least-once means nothing is lost as long as consumers acknowledge after processing, but duplicates can happen, for example if a consumer crashes before acknowledging. At-least-once is the usual default, so consumers must be idempotent, perhaps by recording processed message IDs or using upserts, so a repeat has no extra effect. I would also configure a dead-letter queue, so a poison message moves aside after a number of retries instead of blocking processing, and then alert on it. Ordering is limited too: systems like Kafka only guarantee order within a partition, so I would key related messages together and not assume global order.

text: How do you keep data consistent when one business operation spans several services?
answer: Across services, I avoid distributed transactions like two-phase commit, because they couple services together, hold locks across the network, hurt availability and often are not supported by the data stores involved. Instead, I usually accept eventual consistency and use the saga pattern. A saga breaks the operation into local transactions, each in one service, and if a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps, for example refunding a payment when stock cannot be reserved. It can be choreographed through events or run by an orchestrator, which I prefer for complex flows because the logic is visible in one place. To publish events reliably, I use the outbox pattern: the service writes its business change and the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes it afterwards. That removes the dual-write problem. Delivery is therefore at least once, so every step must be idempotent. Because sagas lack isolation, intermediate states are visible, so I model states like pending explicitly.

text: When do mocks help in a test, and when do they do more harm than good?
expected: fakes or integration tests as alternatives
answer: Mocks help most when I need to isolate a slow, flaky or external dependency, such as a payment provider, an email service or the system clock. They keep unit tests fast and deterministic, and they make it easy to simulate failures like a timeout, which are hard to trigger for real. They do more harm when they tie tests to implementation details. If a test asserts that specific internal methods were called in a certain order, a harmless refactor breaks it even though behavior has not changed. Another danger is mocks drifting from real behavior: the real API changes, the mock does not, and the tests stay green while production breaks. Heavily mocked tests can end up only testing the mocks. So I mock at system boundaries that I do not control, and avoid mocking my own internals. As alternatives, I like fakes, such as an in-memory repository, or integration tests against a real database in a container, and contract tests can keep mocks honest against the real service.

text: What is CI/CD, and what should a good pipeline include?
answer: Continuous integration means developers merge small changes frequently, and every change is automatically built and tested, so problems show up early. Continuous delivery goes further by keeping the code always in a releasable state, with a production release a button press away, while continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically. A good pipeline starts with a build, then linting and type checks, unit tests and integration tests. It should also include security checks such as dependency scanning, secret detection and static analysis. Fast feedback is really important, so I run the quickest checks first, cache dependencies and run tests in parallel, ideally giving developers a result within minutes, because slow pipelines encourage people to batch changes or skip them. After that, the pipeline builds one immutable artifact and promotes that same artifact through staging to production. Deployment itself should be automated, with smoke tests and health checks after release, and with automated rollback if they fail, so that shipping becomes routine and low risk.

text: How do you deploy a new version of a service without downtime?
answer: Before anything else, I would run multiple instances behind a load balancer, then pick a release strategy. A rolling release replaces instances a few at a time. Blue-green brings up a full new environment and switches traffic across at once, which makes rollback very fast but costs more. A canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and increases it while watching error rates and latency. All of these depend on health checks, so an instance only receives traffic once it is ready, and on graceful shutdown to drain in-flight requests. Database changes must be backward compatible, because old and new code run side by side, so I use expand and contract: add a column, deploy, backfill, and remove the old one in a later release. I also keep a clear rollback plan, usually redeploying the previous artifact, with defined metrics that trigger it. Feature flags help by separating deployment from release, so risky behavior can be turned on gradually or off instantly.

text: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container, and how do you keep an image small?
expected: image is a template, container is a running instance
answer: An image is a read-only template containing the application, its dependencies and its configuration, while a container is a running instance of that image, with its own isolated process space and a thin writable layer on top. You can start many containers from one image, a bit like objects from a class. Images are built in layers, with each Dockerfile instruction generally creating one, and Docker caches them. So I put things that rarely change first, like installing dependencies, and application code later, which keeps rebuilds fast. To keep an image small, multi-stage builds are the biggest win: one stage compiles the app with all the build tools, and the final stage copies in only the output needed to run. I also use minimal base images, such as Alpine, a slim variant or distroless, which reduce both size and attack surface. Beyond that, a dockerignore file keeps unneeded files out of the build context, and I leave out development dependencies.

text: Explain what pods, deployments and services are in Kubernetes.
expected: service gives a stable network address
answer: A pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share a network address and can share storage, and most of the time it is just one container, sometimes with a sidecar. Pods are disposable, so you rarely create them directly. A deployment manages them for you: you declare the pod template and how many replicas you want, and it keeps that number running through a replica set. It also handles rollouts, replacing pods gradually when you change the image, and lets you roll back. Since pods come and go and their IP addresses change, a service gives you a stable network address and DNS name, and it load balances across healthy pods matched by labels. Together these give you scaling and self-healing. You can change the replica count by hand or with a horizontal pod autoscaler, and if a pod dies or a liveness probe fails, Kubernetes replaces or restarts it to match the desired state.

text: What is infrastructure as code, and what problems does it solve?
answer: Infrastructure as code means defining things like networks, servers, databases and permissions in versioned files, rather than clicking through a cloud console. A tool such as Terraform lets you declare the desired state, shows a plan of what will change, and then applies it. It solves several problems. First, environments become repeatable, so staging and production can be built from the same definitions and differ only in variables, which also helps with disaster recovery. Second, changes go through code review and have a history in Git, so you can see who changed what and why, and revert if needed. It also replaces undocumented manual steps. The challenges are around state and drift. Terraform keeps a state file mapping your code to real resources, so I would store it remotely with locking and treat it as sensitive, since it can contain secrets. Drift happens when someone changes something by hand, so I would restrict console changes and run regular plans in the pipeline to detect it.

text: What is the difference between logs, metrics and traces, and when do you use each?
expected: traces follow a request across services
using them together during an incident
answer: Logs, metrics and traces answer different questions. Logs record individual events, such as a failed payment with its error message and request ID, so they give detail about what happened in a specific case. I prefer them structured, so they can be searched. Metrics are numbers over time, like request rate, error rate, latency percentiles and memory use. They are cheap to store and aggregate, which makes them ideal for dashboards and alerts, but they tell you little about any one request. Traces follow a single request across services, with spans showing how long each step took, so they are the best way to find where a slow request is spending its time in a distributed system. During an incident, I use them together. A metric alert tells me something is wrong and when it began, a trace shows which service or dependency is responsible, and logs explain exactly why it failed. A shared trace ID across all three makes it easy to jump between them.

text: Error rates spike right after a deployment. What do you do in the first fifteen minutes?
expected: rolling back before finding the root cause
answer: My first step is confirming the impact from dashboards: how high the error rate is, which endpoints and users are affected, and whether the timing truly lines up with the deployment. If it does, I would roll back quickly, before finding the root cause, because restoring service matters more than understanding the failure, and the old version is a known good state. The exception is when a rollback itself is unsafe, for example after a database migration that old code cannot handle, in which case I might disable a feature flag or fix forward. Alongside that, I would communicate status early, naming an incident lead, posting in the incident channel and updating support or customers with what we know and when the next update comes. While that happens, I would check logs and recent changes, including config and dependency updates, since the deployment may be a coincidence. After confirming recovery on the same dashboards, I would schedule a blameless follow-up review with concrete actions.

text: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give a practical example.
expected: a function keeps access to its outer scope
works after the outer function returns
private state or callbacks as an example
answer: A closure is when a function keeps access to variables from its outer scope, and that access keeps working even after the outer function has returned. It happens because JavaScript functions carry a reference to the scope where they were created. A practical example is private state. Say I write a create-counter function that declares a count variable and returns an increment function. Each time I call the returned function, it updates count, and nothing outside can touch that variable directly. Closures are also behind callbacks, event handlers and things like debounce helpers, which remember a timer between calls. There are a couple of pitfalls. Since a closure keeps its variables alive, holding a large object in one that lives a long time, like an event listener never removed, can cause a memory leak. The classic loop problem is another: with var, all the callbacks share one variable and see its final value, while let creates a fresh binding for each iteration, which fixes it.

text: What are the differences between var, let and const in JavaScript?
expected: hoisting and the temporal dead zone
answer: The first difference is scope. Var is function scoped, so a variable declared inside an if block is visible throughout the function, whereas let and const are block scoped and exist only inside the nearest curly braces. The second is hoisting. All three declarations are hoisted, but var is initialized to undefined, so reading it early gives undefined. Let and const stay uninitialized until their declaration runs, and that gap is called the temporal dead zone, so touching them early throws a reference error. The third is reassignment. Var and let can be reassigned, while const cannot, and it must be given a value when declared. Var also allows redeclaring in the same scope, while let and const do not. One common misunderstanding is that const freezes objects, but it only protects the binding. You can still change an object's properties or push to an array, and Object dot freeze is what you would use for that. I default to const, then let, and avoid var.

text: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript, and how do you handle errors with them?
expected: running tasks in parallel with Promise.all
answer: A promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation, and it has three states: pending, fulfilled or rejected. Once it settles, it stays that way. You attach handlers with then and catch, and those run later as microtasks. Async and await are built on promises, so they are mostly nicer syntax. An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses that function until the promise settles, without blocking the main thread, so the code reads top to bottom. For errors, with chains I add a catch handler at the end, and with await I wrap the calls in a try and catch block, since a rejected promise makes await throw. Forgetting either can lead to an unhandled rejection. To run tasks in parallel, I avoid awaiting them one by one and use Promise dot all, which waits for everything and rejects as soon as one fails. If I want every outcome regardless of failures, I use Promise dot all settled instead.

text: How does prototypal inheritance work in JavaScript?
answer: In JavaScript, objects link directly to other objects. Every object has an internal reference to a prototype, which is another object or null. When you read a property, the engine looks on the object itself first, then follows the link to its prototype, and keeps walking up the chain until it finds the property or reaches null, in which case the result is undefined. Writing a property normally creates it on the object itself, shadowing anything further up. Methods therefore live in one shared place rather than being copied to each instance. The class keyword is built on prototypes and is mostly syntax over that mechanism: methods go on the constructor's prototype property, and extends links two prototype chains. The difference from classical inheritance, as in Java, is that there a class is a blueprint and instances are copied from its definition at creation. Here, behavior is delegated at runtime through live objects, so changing a prototype immediately affects every object linked to it.

text: What is event delegation, and why is it useful?
expected: one listener on a parent element
answer: Event delegation relies on the fact that events bubble up the DOM. When you click an element, the event fires on it and then travels up through its ancestors. So instead of attaching a listener to every child, you put one listener on a parent element, and inside the handler you check the event target to see what was actually clicked, usually with the closest method and a selector. Say we have a list of a thousand items, each with a delete button. Rather than a thousand listeners, I would put one on the list itself. This has two main benefits. You get fewer listeners, which saves memory and setup work and makes cleanup simpler. It also works for elements added later, since new items are covered automatically without any wiring. It is worth noting that a few events, such as focus and blur, do not bubble, so you would use focusin and focusout instead, and a stop propagation call further down can block delegation.

text: How does the virtual DOM work in React, and why are keys important in a list?
expected: comparing it with the previous tree
applying the smallest real DOM changes
keys identify list items across renders
answer: When a component renders in React, it does not touch the browser directly. It produces a tree of plain objects describing what the interface should look like, which people call the virtual DOM. On each update, React compares the new tree with the previous one, a process called reconciliation. A full tree comparison would be expensive, so it uses heuristics that make it roughly linear: elements of a different type are replaced entirely, and elements of the same type are updated in place. It then applies the smallest set of real DOM changes needed, batched in a commit phase. Keys matter because they identify list items across renders. With a stable key, like a database ID, React can tell that an item moved rather than changed, so it reuses the element and keeps its state. If you use the array index and the list gets reordered or items are inserted, state such as input text can stick to the wrong row, and you lose performance through needless updates.

text: In a React app, how do you decide where state should live?
expected: keeping state as local as possible
when a state library is worth it
answer: I start by keeping state as local as possible, in the component that actually uses it, because that limits re-renders and makes the code easier to reason about. When two siblings need the same value, I lift it up to their closest common parent and pass it down through props. If that turns into prop drilling across many layers, I might reach for context, but carefully, because every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. So context suits things that change rarely, like the theme or the current user, and splitting contexts or memoizing the value helps. I also separate server state from client state. Data from an API is really a cache of something remote, so a library like TanStack Query handles fetching, caching and revalidation better than hand-rolled state. A dedicated client state library such as Redux or Zustand is worth it when many unrelated components share complex, frequently changing state, and selective subscriptions or debugging tools pay for themselves.

text: What is the difference between reflow and repaint in the browser?
answer: Reflow, also called layout, is when the browser recalculates the size and position of elements, for example after a width change or new content being added. Repaint is when it redraws the pixels for something whose geometry did not change, like a new background color. Reflow is usually more expensive because a change to one element can affect its children, its siblings and sometimes much of the page, and it is normally followed by a repaint anyway. The classic mistake is layout thrashing, where a loop alternates between writing styles and reading values like offset height, which forces the browser to do layout synchronously again and again. I avoid that by batching all the reads together and then all the writes, often inside request animation frame. For animation, I prefer transform and opacity, because the browser can usually handle them on the compositor without triggering layout or paint, whereas animating top or width causes reflow on every frame.

text: A web page loads slowly. How would you find the cause and make it faster?
expected: measuring with browser tools and Core Web Vitals
answer: Before changing anything, I would measure. I would run Lighthouse and look at Core Web Vitals, meaning Largest Contentful Paint for loading, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness and Cumulative Layout Shift for visual stability, ideally with real user data as well as lab results. The network waterfall and performance panel in dev tools then show whether the time goes to a slow server response, heavy assets or long JavaScript tasks. From there, the fix depends on the cause. I would remove render-blocking resources by inlining critical CSS and deferring non-essential scripts. For large bundles, I would use code splitting and lazy load routes and components that are not needed immediately. Images are often the biggest win, so I would compress them, use modern formats like WebP or AVIF, serve responsive sizes and lazy load anything below the fold. Finally, I would serve static assets through a CDN with long cache lifetimes and hashed filenames, then measure again to confirm the improvement.

text: What is semantic HTML, and how does it help accessibility?
answer: Semantic HTML means choosing elements that describe what the content is, not just how it looks. For example, I would use nav, main, article, header and button instead of building everything out of generic divs. This helps accessibility because assistive technology reads that meaning directly. A screen reader can announce a heading level or a button role, and landmarks like main and nav let a user jump straight to a section rather than listening through the whole page. Native elements also bring keyboard support for free. A real button can receive focus and responds to Enter and Space, whereas a clickable div needs a tabindex, key handlers and a role added by hand, and those are easy to get wrong. As for ARIA, I treat it as a backup. I use it only when no native element does the job, like a custom tabs widget, because incorrect ARIA can make the experience worse than having none.

text: What is the difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid, and how do you build a responsive layout?
answer: The main difference is dimensions. Flexbox is one-dimensional, so it lays items out along a single row or column, which makes it great for things like a navigation bar or centering items in a card. Grid is two-dimensional, controlling rows and columns together, so it suits overall page layouts or a gallery where things must line up in both directions. I often use both, with Grid for the page structure and Flexbox inside components. To make a layout responsive, I go mobile-first. I write the base styles for small screens, usually a single column, then add media queries with min-width to adjust the layout as more space becomes available. I also use relative units such as percentages, rem, and viewport units, plus the fr unit in Grid, instead of fixed pixel widths, so that elements adapt naturally to the screen and to the user's font size settings.

text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
expected: aggregates are not allowed in WHERE
answer: Both of them filter, but they run at different stages of a query. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, while HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY and the aggregation are done. Because of that order, you cannot use an aggregate like COUNT or SUM in a WHERE clause, since the groups do not exist yet at that point, and the database will return an error. For example, say we have an orders table with a customer ID, an amount and a status. If I want customers who have spent more than one thousand dollars on completed orders, I would put status equals completed in the WHERE clause to drop the other rows, group by customer ID, and then write HAVING SUM of amount greater than one thousand to keep only the qualifying groups. As a habit, I filter in WHERE whenever I can, because removing rows early usually means less work for the database.

text: What are SQL window functions, and when would you use one instead of GROUP BY?
expected: ranking and running totals as examples
answer: A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows related to the current row, but unlike GROUP BY, it keeps every row instead of collapsing them into one. That is the key difference. If I only need one summary row per group, GROUP BY is the right tool. If I need the detail and the aggregate side by side, I use a window function. You define the window with an OVER clause, where PARTITION BY splits the rows into groups and ORDER BY sets their order inside each group. Say we have an orders table. ROW_NUMBER or RANK partitioned by customer and ordered by date descending lets me pick each customer's latest order. A running total is SUM of amount over the same partition ordered by date. LAG can compare each row with the previous one. Without these, I would need self-joins or correlated subqueries, which are usually harder to read and often slower.

text: What is a p-value, and how is it commonly misunderstood?
expected: probability of data this extreme if the null hypothesis is true
not the probability that the hypothesis is true
answer: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what we observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. So it measures how surprising the data would be if there were really no effect. The most common misunderstanding is reading it as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or that the result happened by chance. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean a three percent chance the null is true, because the calculation assumes the null from the start. To make a decision, we compare it with a significance threshold chosen in advance, commonly 0.05, and reject the null if it falls below. That threshold is a convention, not a magic line. I also separate statistical significance from practical significance. With a very large sample, a tiny effect can give a small p-value and still not matter to the business, so I always look at the effect size and its confidence interval too.

text: Explain the central limit theorem and why it matters.
expected: distribution of sample means approaches normal
regardless of the original distribution in most cases
basis for confidence intervals and tests
answer: The central limit theorem says that if you take many random samples of the same size from a population and compute each sample's mean, the distribution of those means gets closer to a normal distribution as the sample size grows. What makes it powerful is that this holds regardless of the original distribution in most cases, as long as the observations are independent and the variance is finite. So even skewed data, like revenue per user, gives approximately normal sample means. Larger samples help in two ways.
